design_detail: Randomized, double-blind, two-period crossover laboratory study in a cardiovascular physiology laboratory in Dallas, Texas: 7 healthy volunteers who had never used cocaine or other drugs recreationally each underwent passive whole-body heating twice, 3 to 6 days apart at the same time of day, once after intranasal cocaine hydrochloride and once after intranasal lidocaine hydrochloride (the active control for cocaine's local anaesthetic effect, called 'placebo' in the abstract). Heating was supine, in a tube-lined suit perfused with water at 46°C, for about 38 minutes as plotted in Figure 1 (the duration is not stated in the text). Outcomes: esophageal and skin temperature, forearm skin blood flow (as cutaneous vascular conductance), forearm sweat rate, heart rate, blood pressure and rated thermal sensation.
can_establish: That in these 7 healthy people who had never used cocaine, a single low intranasal dose given before passive heating, compared with lidocaine, raised the core temperatures at which skin vasodilation and sweating began, reduced both at a given core temperature, was followed by a larger rise in core temperature, and lowered how hot people felt at a given core temperature.
cannot_establish: Whether impaired heat loss rather than greater heat production is the main cause of hyperthermia in people who use cocaine (heat production was not measured; one low dose; passive heating at rest); whether the same happens in people who use cocaine regularly, at the doses and routes used outside the laboratory, or with exertion; and anything about how often hyperthermia or death occurs.

sample.recruitment: Healthy volunteers; how they were recruited is not reported (p. 786, Methods › Participants).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Normotensive, with no history of cardiovascular disease, cocaine use or other recreational drug use, and no prescription or non-prescription drugs with cardiovascular or autonomic effects. No smoking and no alcohol- or caffeine-containing drinks for at least 12 hours before each experiment (p. 786, Methods › Participants).
sample.demographics: Men and women aged 23 to 37; the number of each sex, body size and fitness are not reported (p. 786).
sample.attrition: No withdrawals are reported; the results are presented as from all 7 in both conditions. The number contributing at the highest core temperatures and at each thermal-sensation rating is not reported (see reporting issues).
sample.selection_effects: Seven healthy young volunteers with no drug experience, chosen so that cocaine's effect could be studied without the effects of long-term use; they are not representative of people who use cocaine, which the authors acknowledge (p. 790).

exposure.measurement: Study drug given by the investigators: intranasal cocaine hydrochloride or lidocaine hydrochloride, each 2 mg/kg of body weight as a 10% solution (p. 787, Methods › Experimental Protocol).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Study conditions only: one intranasal dose of 2 mg/kg in each session, described by the authors as half the standard dose for rhinolaryngological procedures (p. 787) and as low and non-euphoric (pp. 786, 790); the absence of euphoria was not measured in this study but cited from the authors' earlier work (reference 11). Passive heating at rest, supine, with no exercise. These conditions differ from use outside the laboratory, where doses, routes, repetition, exertion and other drugs vary, as the authors note (p. 790).
exposure.polysubstance: None: participants had no recreational drug use, took no medicines with cardiovascular or autonomic effects, and abstained from tobacco, alcohol and caffeine for at least 12 hours (p. 786).
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Not applicable (participants had never used cocaine). Sessions 3 to 6 days apart (p. 787).

comparison.controls: The same participants after intranasal lidocaine 2 mg/kg, used as a control for cocaine's local anaesthetic action (p. 787). No inert placebo condition and no condition without heating were run.
comparison.matching: Within-person crossover; both sessions at the same time of day; skin temperature rose similarly in both, which the authors take as evidence that the heat stress was the same (p. 788; Figure 1, top).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not applicable to a within-person comparison; heat acclimatization, fitness and body composition, which affect heat loss, were not reported.
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Not applicable (within-person design; no recreational drug use by entry criterion).

outcomes.instruments: Esophageal temperature by thermistor at a depth of 25% of standing height; mean skin temperature from six thermocouples; forearm skin blood flow by laser Doppler flowmetry, expressed as cutaneous vascular conductance (Doppler signal divided by mean arterial pressure) as a percentage of the maximum obtained by local heating to 42°C for 30 minutes after the heat stress; forearm sweat rate by ventilated capsule (2.8 cm²); heart rate by electrocardiogram; blood pressure by oscillometry; thermal sensation on a 9-point scale from 4.0 (neutral) to 8.0 (unbearably hot) in steps of 0.5 (pp. 786–787, Methods › Measurements and Experimental Protocol).
outcomes.validity_norms: Standard thermoregulatory physiology methods. The authors cite a test–retest variability of 0.09°C for the sweating threshold from another study (p. 789). The forearm used for blood flow was outside the heating suit, so local heating did not drive its blood flow (p. 786).
outcomes.operationalization: 'Impaired heat dissipation' was read from the esophageal temperature at which cutaneous vascular conductance and sweat rate began to rise (the threshold, picked from individual plots), the slope of their rise against esophageal temperature, and their values at the 'highest common esophageal temperature' of 37.86°C. 'Impaired heat perception' was read as a higher esophageal temperature at the same thermal-sensation rating (p. 787, Data Collection and Statistical Analysis).
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None; alpha 0.05 for every test (p. 787). Editors' count of the comparisons reported: 4 before heating, 2 at the end of heating, 4 whole-curve analyses of variance, 2 values at 37.86°C, 2 thresholds, 2 slopes and 6 thermal-sensation ratings (5.0 to 7.5).
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Double-blind by design; the investigator who identified the thresholds was blinded to participant and condition (p. 787). Whether participants could tell cocaine from lidocaine was not assessed, although cocaine raised blood pressure and heart rate before heating (p. 787).

analysis.effect_sizes: Means (±SE), cocaine against lidocaine (pp. 787–788). Before heating: esophageal temperature 36.79 ± 0.01 against 36.75 ± 0.08°C (no difference); mean arterial pressure 93 ± 3 against 85 ± 3 mm Hg, P=0.001; heart rate 74 ± 5 against 67 ± 4 beats/min, P=0.01; cutaneous vascular conductance 9 ± 2 against 7 ± 2% of maximum, P=0.09. End of heating: mean arterial pressure 92 ± 2 against 87 ± 2 mm Hg, P<0.01; heart rate 107 ± 5 against 105 ± 5 beats/min, P>0.2. Esophageal temperature rose more with cocaine during heating, P<0.001; no number is given in the text, and read from Figure 1 (approximate) it ended at about 37.8°C with cocaine and 37.5°C with lidocaine after about 38 minutes, from about 36.8°C in both. Thresholds: vasodilation 37.37 ± 0.09 against 37.06 ± 0.07°C, P=0.01; sweating 37.38 ± 0.09 against 37.07 ± 0.06°C, P=0.002; slopes unchanged. At 37.86°C: cutaneous vascular conductance 49 ± 9 against 70 ± 5% of maximum, P=0.03; sweat rate 0.8 ± 0.2 against 1.0 ± 0.1 mg/cm² per minute, P=0.04. Editors' calculation, back-calculated from the printed (rounded) P values of the paired t-tests with 6 df, so approximate: threshold shift 0.31°C for both, 95% CI about 0.11 to 0.51°C (vasodilation) and 0.16 to 0.46°C (sweating), paired standardized differences (dz) about 1.4 and 2.0; difference in conductance at 37.86°C 21 percentage points (about 3 to 39) and in sweat rate 0.2 mg/cm² per minute (about 0.01 to 0.39), assuming all 7 contributed at that temperature.
analysis.covariates: None (within-person comparison). Treatment order was included in the models and had no effect on any outcome (p. 787).
analysis.preregistration_detail: No registration or protocol is cited (2002).
analysis.selective_reporting: The headline result (a greater rise in core temperature) is given only as P<0.001 and a figure; the comparison at 37.86°C is not explained (see reporting issues). No outcome appears to have been left unreported, but there is no protocol to check against.
analysis.power: Not reported. Seven participants; the intervals for the threshold shifts exclude zero, but the comparisons at 37.86°C have lower limits close to no difference.

interpretation_gap.results_show: In 7 healthy people who had never used cocaine, heated at rest in a suit perfused with water at 46°C, one intranasal dose of cocaine (2 mg/kg) compared with lidocaine did not change core temperature before heating, raised the core temperature at which skin vasodilation and sweating began by about 0.3°C (more than three times the 0.09°C test–retest variability the authors cite), reduced skin vascular conductance and sweat rate at 37.86°C, was followed by a larger rise in core temperature during heating, and left people feeling less hot at the same core temperature.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract concludes that "impaired heat dissipation is a major mechanism by which cocaine elevates body temperature" in humans (p. 785), and the Discussion that impaired heat dissipation rather than greater heat production was the dominant mechanism (p. 789). Gaps: (1) heat production was not measured; the inference rests on the absence of a temperature change before heating at a dose the authors call too low to cause euphoria, and they themselves expect larger doses to add heat production (p. 790). (2) The results come from 7 cocaine-naive people at rest, which the authors acknowledge may not apply to people with long-term use (p. 790). (3) The Discussion calls the pattern a property of cocaine not shared by methamphetamine or ephedrine (p. 790), but no other drug was tested; this rests on cited studies. (4) The introduction states as established that the rise in overdose deaths in hot weather is specific to cocaine and not seen with opiates (p. 785, citing Marzuk et al., 1998), a claim that rested on non-significant comparisons in that paper. (5) 'Substantially augmented' (abstract) is not quantified in the text. The speculation that the effect is greatly amplified in hot weather, crowded nightclubs and raves is labelled as speculation (p. 790).

timeline.event: Epidemiological basis cited by the authors: more cocaine overdose deaths on hot days in New York City

Published letter on this paper with the authors' reply (Schier et al., 2002, 'Cocaine and body temperature regulation', Annals of Internal Medicine; on the project's reading list; not among the files read for this card).

replication.where_it_stands: Provisional: no replication was read for this card, and later laboratory studies of cocaine and thermoregulation were not searched by this reader. The study is a single small mechanistic experiment from one laboratory; its central measurements (threshold shifts) are consistent within the paper, and the critique in the published letter and the authors' reply should be read before the card is relied on.

funding.funder: National Institutes of Health (HL-61388) (Dr. Crandall); the American Heart Association, Texas Affiliate (0060010Y) (Dr. Vongpatanasin); and the National Institute on Drug Abuse (RO-1 DA10064) (Dr. Victor). The funding sources had no role in design, analysis, interpretation or the decision to submit (pp. 787, 790).
funding.declared_conflicts: Potential financial conflicts of interest: none disclosed (p. 790).
funding.affiliations_note: University of Texas Southwestern Medical Center and the Institute for Exercise and Environmental Medicine, Presbyterian Hospital of Dallas (p. 790). The authors' own earlier study is the source for the dose being non-euphoric and for cocaine's central sympathetic action (reference 11). Recorded as a flag for closer reading, not as a reason to discount the results.

what_would_settle_it: A registered, adequately powered randomized crossover study in people who already use cocaine, at more than one dose, with an inert placebo as well as lidocaine, measuring heat production (by indirect calorimetry) alongside skin blood flow, sweating and core temperature, during both passive heating and exercise, with the blinding checked and every participant's data reported at each core temperature.

domains.note: Order was randomized, but how the sequence was generated and concealed, and how many people received each order, are not reported. Core temperature and skin blood flow before heating were similar in the two sessions.

domains.domain: Bias arising from period and carryover effects (crossover)
domains.note: Sessions 3 to 6 days apart at the same time of day; treatment order was included in the models and had no effect on any outcome, although with 7 people that test has little power.

Double-blind with an active local-anaesthetic control, but cocaine raised blood pressure and heart rate before heating and blinding was not checked; this matters most for the self-rated thermal sensation.

No withdrawals reported, but the number of participants contributing at 37.86°C and at each sensation rating is not given; the lidocaine mean core temperature ended below 37.86°C, and Figure 3 has no cocaine value at the top rating.

Core temperature, skin blood flow and sweat rate are instrument measures, and thresholds were picked by an investigator blinded to condition. Thermal sensation is self-rated and depends on blinding (see deviations).
No protocol or registration; about 22 comparisons without correction; the 'highest common esophageal temperature' at which conductance and sweat rate were compared is not defined in the methods.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: A small, carefully instrumented within-person experiment whose main measurements are objective and whose thresholds were read blind. Concerns are the unreported randomization details, the unchecked blinding (relevant to the perception result), the unclear number of participants behind the comparisons at the highest temperatures, and the absence of a protocol. The card may be cited for what one low intranasal dose did to heat-loss responses and thermal perception in 7 healthy cocaine-naive people under passive heating; not for the size of the effect in people who use cocaine, for heat production, or for risk in hot weather.

key_findings.finding: Before heating, cocaine did not change esophageal temperature compared with lidocaine (36.79 ± 0.01 against 36.75 ± 0.08°C, mean ± SE) but raised mean arterial pressure (93 ± 3 against 85 ± 3 mm Hg, P=0.001) and heart rate (74 ± 5 against 67 ± 4 beats/min, P=0.01); skin vascular conductance did not differ significantly (9 ± 2 against 7 ± 2% of maximum, P=0.09). n=7, each in both conditions.

During heating, heart rate rose in both conditions (to 107 ± 5 with cocaine and 105 ± 5 beats/min with lidocaine, P>0.2), mean arterial pressure did not rise, and at the end of heating it was still higher with cocaine (92 ± 2 against 87 ± 2 mm Hg, P<0.01). Skin temperature rose similarly in both conditions.
key_findings.locator: Results, 2nd paragraph (p. 787, continuing on p. 788); Figure 1, top (p. 788)

key_findings.finding: Esophageal temperature rose more during heating after cocaine than after lidocaine (P<0.001, two-way repeated-measures analysis of variance). The text gives no size for the difference.
key_findings.note: Read from a 300-dpi enlargement of Figure 1 (approximate): from about 36.8°C in both conditions to about 37.8°C with cocaine and about 37.5°C with lidocaine after about 38 minutes of heating; the curves begin to separate around 10 minutes.

key_findings.finding: Cocaine raised the esophageal temperature at which skin vasodilation began (37.37 ± 0.09 against 37.06 ± 0.07°C, P=0.01) and at which sweating began (37.38 ± 0.09 against 37.07 ± 0.06°C, P=0.002), with no change in the slopes of either response.
key_findings.note: Editors' calculation from the rounded P values (paired t-test, 6 df): a shift of 0.31°C, 95% CI about 0.11 to 0.51°C (vasodilation) and 0.16 to 0.46°C (sweating).

key_findings.finding: At the 'highest common esophageal temperature' of 37.86°C, skin vascular conductance was 49 ± 9% of maximum with cocaine against 70 ± 5% with lidocaine (P=0.03), and sweat rate 0.8 ± 0.2 against 1.0 ± 0.1 mg/cm² per minute (P=0.04).
key_findings.note: How many participants contributed at 37.86°C is not reported (see reporting issues).

key_findings.finding: Cocaine lessened the rise in thermal discomfort although core temperature rose more: the esophageal temperature at each perceived-heating rating from 5.0 to 7.5 (on a scale of 4.0, neutral, to 8.0, unbearably hot) was compared by paired t-tests, and the difference first became significant above 37.0°C and widened as core temperature rose (P<0.05).
key_findings.locator: Methods › Measurements, 2nd paragraph (p. 786); Statistical Analysis (p. 787); Results, 3rd paragraph (p. 788); Figure 3 (p. 789)
key_findings.note: Read from a 300-dpi enlargement of Figure 3 (approximate): the asterisks mark ratings 5.5 to 7.5; at 'very hot' (7.0), about 37.4°C with lidocaine and 37.7°C with cocaine. Figure 3 shows a lidocaine value at 'unbearably hot' (8.0), about 37.8°C, and no cocaine value at that rating.

key_findings.finding: The authors cite a test–retest variability of 0.09°C for the sweating threshold (from another study) and state that cocaine raised both thresholds by more than three times that.

Study conditions: intranasal cocaine hydrochloride or lidocaine hydrochloride, 2 mg/kg as a 10% solution, given before passive whole-body heating with water at 46°C in a tube-lined suit, supine, in sessions 3 to 6 days apart; the cocaine dose is described as half the standard dose for rhinolaryngological procedures.
key_findings.locator: Methods › Experimental Protocol (p. 786, continuing on p. 787)

key_findings.finding: The authors state that the effect was seen at a very low dose that did not produce euphoria (citing their earlier study), that larger doses would be expected to add heat production, and that results from healthy cocaine-naive people may not apply to people with long-term cocaine use.
The authors speculate, without testing it, that hot weather, crowded nightclubs and raves would greatly amplify cocaine's effect on body temperature.

Background stated in the introduction, not data from this study: fatal cocaine overdose is typically associated with blood cocaine of 3 to 6 mg/L, while deaths with hyperthermia can occur at levels 10 to 20 times lower.
key_findings.note: Second-hand (Escobedo et al., 1991; Kosten & Kleber, 1988, the paper's references 1 and 2); a claim about post-mortem levels should cite those sources, not this paper.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract calls the control 'placebo (lidocaine, 2 mg/kg)' and the design placebo-controlled, but lidocaine is an active local anaesthetic, used, as the Methods say, to control for cocaine's local anaesthetic property; no inert placebo was given.
reporting_issues.consequence: The comparison isolates effects of cocaine beyond local anaesthesia; it cannot exclude an effect of lidocaine itself on the outcomes.

reporting_issues.issue: The headline result, a greater rise in core temperature with cocaine, is given in the text only as P<0.001 with no magnitude; its size has to be read from Figure 1.
reporting_issues.consequence: Claims should use the figure reading with its approximation stated (about 0.2 to 0.3°C at the end of heating), not 'substantially'.

reporting_issues.issue: Conductance and sweat rate were compared at the 'highest common esophageal temperature' of 37.86°C, which the Methods do not define; in Figure 1 the mean lidocaine core temperature ends at about 37.5°C, so not every participant can have reached 37.86°C under lidocaine, and the number contributing is not given. The curve ends in Figure 2 (about 67% and 54% of maximum, read from the figure) also differ somewhat from the values in the text (70% and 49%).
reporting_issues.consequence: The P values of 0.03 and 0.04 may rest on fewer than 7 people; the comparison at that temperature should be cited with this caveat.

reporting_issues.issue: The legend of Figure 2 marks the cocaine–lidocaine difference at P<0.01, while the text gives P=0.03 (conductance) and P=0.04 (sweat rate) for the same responses; the test behind the legend (presumably the whole-curve analysis of variance) is not stated.
reporting_issues.consequence: Two different P values describe the same panel; cite the text values for the comparison at 37.86°C.

reporting_issues.issue: The standard error of the pre-heating esophageal temperature with cocaine is printed as ±0.01°C, against ±0.08°C with lidocaine; with 7 people this implies a between-person SD of about 0.03°C (editors' calculation), implausibly small beside the 0.21°C implied for the other session.
reporting_issues.consequence: Possibly a typographical error; it does not affect the conclusion that cocaine did not change core temperature before heating.

reporting_issues.issue: The duration of heating and the rule for stopping it are not stated; Figure 1 plots about 38 minutes in both conditions, and Figure 3 shows a lidocaine value at 'unbearably hot' with no cocaine value at that rating.
reporting_issues.consequence: If heating was stopped by tolerance or time, the end-of-heating comparisons depend on it; the paper does not allow this to be checked.

reporting_issues.issue: The thermal-sensation scale is anchored at 4.0 as 'neutral' in the Methods but labelled 'Comfortable' in Figure 3, whose legend says the ratings were modified from the source scale; the number of men and women among the 7 is not reported.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; the scale's anchors and the sample's composition cannot be fully checked.

verification.source_read: PDF (version of record), Ann Intern Med 136(11), pp. 785–791 (all pages; Figures 1–3 checked on rendered pages, Figures 1 to 3 also enlarged at 300 dpi and the values marked as read from them are approximate; no table; no supplement; the author contributions said to be online were not available). The published letter with the authors' reply (Schier et al., 2002, 10.7326/0003-4819-137-10-200211190-00017) was not among the files read.
